{"id": "2:32/q16", "question": "What does “al-ʿAlīm” mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the name's scope is stated generally or applied to the angels' hidden thoughts.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q16/p1", "position": "God knows comprehensively without being taught, including hidden, past, and future things.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says God needs no teacher; Ibn ʿAbbās calls His knowledge perfect. Ibn Isḥāq specifies what angels conceal; Baghawī says His creation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Qurṭubī emphasize the intensive faʿīl form. Rāzī says only God merits it absolutely. Bayḍāwī says nothing is hidden; Bursawī connects it with 2:30."}, {"id": "2:32/q16/p2", "position": "It specifically points to God's knowledge of the angels' concealed claim.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq glosses the name by what they hide; Bayḍāwī says God knows the hidden conditions of heaven and earth, including theirs. Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas reports that God exposed the angels' concealed claim to superior knowledge and honor."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q25", "question": "What did the angels' inability demonstrate about Adam and vicegerency?", "turns_on": "Whether knowledge of names by itself establishes fitness, or deeper human representation is needed.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q25/p1", "position": "Adam's taught knowledge showed his fitness and rank over the angels.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī says God raised Adam by the names; Bayḍāwī calls knowledge central to vicegerency and superior to worship, citing 39:9. Nasafī says names knowledge surpasses worship, even more so divine law. Elmalılı and al-Sāmarrāʾī say the comparison tested Adam's fitness and prepared angelic submission. Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas says God taught Adam the names to show his superiority over the angels who privately boasted of theirs."}, {"id": "2:32/q25/p2", "position": "The angels' failure alone cannot establish unfitness for succession; a deeper representative capacity matters.", "reasons": "Elmalılı argues that ignorance of all names would imply no speech, while ignorance of descendants' or new names would not disqualify them. Human representative speech and direct angelic cognition differ; humans can also err by confusing words or concepts with truth."}, {"id": "2:32/q25/p3", "position": "Adam's comprehensive inward and outward constitution makes him uniquely representative of God.", "reasons": "Bursawī says he gathers spiritual, bodily, celestial and earthly realms, uniquely received God's spirit (17:70), and mirrors divine attributes. Angels know God yet not themselves and all attributes; the human inner lamp images the spirit's manifestation in just and merciful action, citing 38:26, 9:128, 48:29."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q26", "question": "What does the scene imply about the origin of language and the angels' speech?", "turns_on": "Whether 'teaching names' concerns prior divine designation or how angelic communication itself occurs.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q26/p1", "position": "God instituted the names and their meanings before Adam used them.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī reasons that teaching words with meanings presupposes prior designation, and no creature before Adam could designate them. Ibn Isḥāq says Adam named every thing and the names he gave those things endure until the Resurrection."}, {"id": "2:32/q26/p2", "position": "Angelic dialogue is direct illumination or knowledge, unlike human indirect representative speech.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says angels' speech cannot be ordinary naming whether they lacked all names or just some; God first addressed them by direct reality and their glorification likewise expresses illumination. Adam's speech conveys knowledge indirectly via signs or deputies."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q27", "question": "How does this passage connect to God's previous claim to know what the angels did not?", "turns_on": "How the scene functions in the surrounding narrative and later address.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q27/p1", "position": "The names test and its answer display the hidden knowledge and wisdom asserted in 2:30.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī says the follow-up challenge restates the 2:30 claim in fuller form and exposes hidden conditions. Bursawī links al-ʿAlīm to that claim; Abū Ḥayyān says Adam's learning reveals why God appointed him. Ṭabarī's continuation relates the naming and the angels' reply to God's disclosure of Iblis's concealed pride, mentioning 38:75 and 7:12–13; al-Rabīʿ b. Anas relates the test to the angels' hidden boast, citing the surrounding 2:31–33."}, {"id": "2:32/q27/p2", "position": "The story prepares the audience for the call to the Children of Israel.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says divine lordship and embedded human gifts lead into 2:40; Ṭabarī says the account recalls favors to their ancestors and warns of Iblis-like punishment for continued rebellion."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q29", "question": "What report explains the angels' prior private claim and subsequent repentance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q29/p1", "position": "They expected no creature more knowledgeable or honored; Adam's knowledge and commanded prostration corrected them.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān transmits their expectation. Al-Durr reports Qatāda and al-Ḥasan that the angels privately claimed superiority and repented when unable to answer. Al-Baghawī's report says prostration was ordered after Adam's spirit was breathed, citing 15:29. Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas also reports that the angels privately boasted of superior knowledge and honor and that Adam's names exposed the claim."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q34", "question": "What lesson for believers does the angels' repentance convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q34/p1", "position": "Every believer should resort to repentance, as the angels did when confessing their dependence on God's teaching.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda report the angels' repentance and say that every believer resorts to repentance."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q01", "question": "What occasion prompted the command to take charity?", "turns_on": "Whether the command addresses the repentant stay-behinds, Abū Lubāba alone, or a different alms episode.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q01/p1", "position": "Repentant men who stayed behind offered their wealth; the Prophet awaited revelation, then accepted charity.", "reasons": "Muqātil says three men brought the wealth that held them back. Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd, and later exegetes connect the offer to release from mosque pillars and 9:102; some report he took a third. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates their gift to repairing Tabūk losses. Al-Biqāʿī calls it confirmation of accepted repentance. Qatāda confirms the Tabūk group. Elmalılı allows that the Prophet's initial refusal concerned earlier refusal of alms from people such as Ḥāṭib ibn Saʿlaba. Al-Qurṭubī reports that the command was revealed after someone said the Prophet had not been ordered to take anything from their wealth."}, {"id": "9:103/q01/p2", "position": "The command arose from Abū Lubāba's repentance over warning Banū Qurayẓa by pointing to his throat.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and al-Bāqir identify him alone; reports describe his binding himself to a pillar and fasting until forgiven. Al-Zuhrī instead connects his binding and seven days of abstention to missing Tabūk."}, {"id": "9:103/q01/p3", "position": "A report connects the verse to Thaʿlaba's refusal to pay alms, contrasted with a man of Sulaym who willingly gave good camels.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports Thaʿlaba called the collectors' demand a tax."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q04", "question": "What does 'take' mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q04/p1", "position": "It means accept the offered charity.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī lists covenant, judgment, alms and pardon as senses of acceptance, while a cited passage denies acceptance of ransom. The Prophet's delay until revelation shows the issue was authorization to accept. Al-Qurṭubī reports the intervening statement that no order to take their wealth had yet been given before the command was revealed."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q06", "question": "How does 'from their wealth' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Its attachment to the verb or to the following indefinite charity.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q06/p1", "position": "Min is partitive and the phrase attaches to 'take'.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this strongest; al-Ṭabrisī says all wealth need not be given. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow attachment to the verb. Reported one-third collections illustrate partitivity. Al-Ṭabrisī explicitly infers the one-third taking from 'from their wealth' rather than an order to take all of it."}, {"id": "9:103/q06/p2", "position": "The phrase modifies 'charity' as an advanced circumstantial expression.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says it was originally an adjective of ṣadaqa and advanced; al-Ālūsī allows an omitted circumstantial modifier."}]}
{"id": "20:10/q04", "question": "What was reported about the tree and fire as Moses approached?", "turns_on": "Reports give different tree species and details of its behavior; al-Rāzī questions whether the Qurʾānic wording establishes any tree.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q04/p1", "position": "The fire appeared in a green tree and did not consume it.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī describes brilliant white fire surrounding the tree from bottom to top without altering its green color; Ibn ʿAbbās marveled at its unchanged beauty. Al-Mahdawī says it receded as Moses approached, then drew near after fear. Al-Qushayrī says the tree burned end to end but yielded no flame and illuminated hearts, while al-Rāzī notes the Qurʾān does not establish the tree detail. Wahb ibn Munabbih reports a great fire growing within the lush green tree without consuming it; when Moses attempted to take a flame, it retreated and went out. Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Wahb's account of a white glow like fire in the green tree, accompanied by angelic praise and brilliant light; Moses felt fear, then calm, before being called."}, {"id": "

20:10/q04/p2", "position": "The tree was a jujube or ʿanāb.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported for the jujube identification; Abū Ḥayyān's collected variants include ʿanāb."}, {"id": "20:10/q04/p3", "position": "The tree was al-ʿawsaj, a thorn tree.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Muqātil and al-Kalbī are named by al-Baghawī; al-Mahdawī says a thorn tree."}, {"id": "20:10/q04/p4", "position": "The tree was a green samura.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī attributes this to Ibn Masʿūd; Abū Ḥayyān lists it among variants."}, {"id": "20:10/q04/p5", "position": "The tree was al-ʿaliq or ʿalīqah.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī reports Wahb's identification; Abū Ḥayyān lists the variant. Wahb ibn Munabbih identifies the green tree containing the fire as al-ʿaliq."}, {"id": "20:10/q04/p6", "position": "Moses thought the distant light was a shepherd's fire.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī and Bursevī connect the expectation of a firebrand to shepherds."}]}
{"id": "20:10/q14", "question": "What is the 'qabas' Moses hopes to bring?", "turns_on": "Whether qabas is specifically a flaming brand, as al-Ālūsī insists, or may also be called an ember.", "positions": [{"id": "20:10/q14/p1", "position": "A flame or burning brand taken from a larger fire, carried on a stick or wick for warmth.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj specify the tip of a stick or reed, and al-Zajjāj allows a wick; al-Samīn calls it a passive-sense verbal noun, a glowing end taken up. Al-Ālūsī equates it with the jadwah of 28:29 and distinguishes it from an ember. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts its guiding warmth with hostile meteors and notes iqtabasa at 57:13; a report from al-Bāqir says the family needed warmth. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes a flame taken from a burning source, such as a firebrand, and infers darkness and no means of kindling their own fire. Al-Thaʿlabī allows the flame to be taken from wood, reed, or another material."}, {"id": "20:10/q14/p2", "position": "An ember or piece of fire to carry back.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow an ember, and Ibn Kathīr cites 28:29 for a glowing brand and warmth; Iṣlāḥī likewise speaks of an ember against cold. Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly includes an ember or coal among what can be taken as a qabas."}]}
{"id": "20:13/q19", "question": "What adjacent reports concern God's speech to Moses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:13/q19/p1", "position": "God spoke to Moses twice, while Muhammad saw his Lord twice and Adam disobeyed twice.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports this from Kaʿb without grading it."}, {"id": "20:13/q19/p2", "position": "Before the call, Moses saw a green tree glowing white like fire amid angelic praise and brilliant light; he feared, then became calm.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports Wahb b. Munabbih's description of the scene before Moses was called."}]}
{"id": "20:13/q24", "question": "What does the predication in 'I chose you' accomplish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:13/q24/p1", "position": "It reinforces the surprising announcement of choice so Moses will not doubt it; it does not restrict the assertion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that verbal predication strengthens unexpected news without making it exclusive. Al-Thaʿlabī says repeating the pronoun intensifies the sign, removes doubt, and establishes certain recognition; he also mentions 15:89."}]}
{"id": "20:49/q23", "question": "What implied question does قَالَ answer here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:49/q23/p1", "position": "It answers an implied question asking what Pharaoh said in reply; a question is best answered with a verb.", "reasons": "Burhān explains Qur'anic 'he said' clauses as answers to omitted questions, citing Pharaoh's question about God and comparing other passages such as 11:69, 15:57, and 36:13."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q04", "question": "What does God give each thing as its 'creation'?", "turns_on": "Whether khalq is form, counterpart, useful endowment, provision, or existence, and how the objects of 'gave' are construed.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q04/p1", "position": "He gives each being its distinctive, fitting form and constitution.", "reasons": "Mujāhid distinguishes human and animal kinds and links measured creation to 25:2; al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq stress the most useful form; Ibn ʿAbbās says God perfects what He creates. Al-Biqāʿī includes shape, size, color, temperament, benefits and effects; Asad includes inner nature and outer form. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes genera, species, classes and individuals. Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī cite poetry using khalq for form. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr adds fitting mating and that creatures do not control their own creation, provision or mating. Al-Qurṭubī says the wording embraces all reported interpretations. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī (TABATABAI:6:122-127/r1) states that God gives each thing its form before directing it toward its created perfection."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p2", "position": "He gives each creature a corresponding mate of its own kind.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ pairs human male with woman, sheep with sheep, and bull with cow; al-Kalbī gives man/woman and camel/she-camel; al-Thaʿlabī and Saʿīd give horse/mare and donkey/female. Al-Ṭabarī says unlike species are not paired and construes an omitted 'like' by analogy with calling a person a lion. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī's reported view cites 51:49. Ibn Qutayba includes sexed form within fitting form. Al-Ālūsī treats pairing as an example, questioning a literal universal."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p3", "position": "He gives each thing what suits, repairs, perfects or benefits it.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda describe fitness and well-being; al-Ḍaḥḥāk illustrates with useful organs. Al-Wāḥidī says its form suits its purpose. Al-Ālūsī says individuals remain complete in their rank despite defects, invoking 32:7 and 67:3 and Sunni teaching that wise creation is grace, not obligation."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p4", "position": "He equips creatures with the faculties and organs proper to their functions.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk's examples are hands for grasping, feet for walking, tongues for speech, eyes for sight and ears for hearing. Al-Wāḥidī understands 'creation' as the things created in bodily organs; al-Qushayrī places the created faculties in limbs. Al-Rāzī adds the coordinated powers of a body."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p5", "position": "He gives every creature everything it needs or can use.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and later grammarians connect this to reversing the two objects of 'gave'; al-Bayḍāwī says the advanced object is the point being explained. Al-Jubbāʾī includes worldly blessings and religious guidance; Abū Muslim includes what people possess. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 6:99. Al-Ālūsī finds the usual object order clearer; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects narrowing 'everything' to blessings and 'creation' to creatures."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p6", "position": "He gives each creature inspired knowledge or craft.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī report this further explanation."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p7", "position": "He gives each thing existence itself or its created reality.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes khalq as bringing into existence; al-Samīn reports a gloss that God originated each thing. A reported account in al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes existence accord with disposition; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects it as contextually remote."}, {"id": "20:50/q04/p8", "position": "He gives each creature its soul.", "reasons": "The report from Ibn ʿAbbās places the soul before guidance to mate, food, drink and dwelling."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q07", "question": "Does 'every thing' cover individuals or kinds?", "turns_on": "Whether incidental defects and the past tense limit a universal statement.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q07/p1", "position": "It covers every individual in its fitting rank.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects restricting it because incidental defects do not undo each thing's completeness in its own rank; he cites 32:7 and 67:3 and says past tense does not establish a restriction. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows distributive generality: each receives its own creation as each rider mounts their own animal. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues unqualified wording extends guidance to everything. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī (TABATABAI:6:122-127/r1) expressly applies creational guidance to each kind and each individual, including its appointed course and lifespan."}, {"id": "20:50/q07/p2", "position": "It denotes kinds, or conventional generality limited to suitable recipients.", "reasons": "Some in al-Ālūsī invoke defective individuals; al-Ālūsī counters that even if many individuals do not yet exist, already existing kinds do not settle the past-tense objection. Ibn ʿĀshūr permits conventional generality; the animal-mate explanation likewise takes 'all' as abundance."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q08", "question": "To what does God guide creatures?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance is general practical direction, mating instinct, the universal movement toward an end, religious guidance, destiny, or a later faculty.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q08/p1", "position": "He directs each creature toward its needs, welfare and livelihood.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda and Yahyā speak of learned benefit and taking what is needed; al-Suddī and Muqātil specify pasture and food, with grain and meat differing by animal. Ibn Qutayba includes avoiding danger; Ibn ʿAbbās lists food, drink, dwelling, birth and mates. Al-Rāzī adds refining materials, preparing medicines and food, bees' hexagonal cells, and offspring finding mothers' breasts. Al-Ḥasan connects guidance to what makes a thing sound; Abū Isḥāq and al-Zajjāj include mating within the broader welfare sense. Al-Qurṭubī says general wording encompasses the explanations, and Ibn Qutayba says their senses relate."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p2", "position": "He inspires creatures to find and approach their mates.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba stress instinctive intercourse; al-Zajjāj says males approach females without instruction. Ibn ʿAbbās adds aff

This is included in the broader welfare reading according to Abū Isḥāq and al-Zajjāj."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p3", "position": "He guides beings to their created ends and fullest attainable development.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī distinguishes instinct from choice and preservation from perfection; al-Burūsawī links equipment to purpose. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines guidance as showing or conveying a thing to its goal: innate powers produce its effects, as an embryo becomes a human; interacting systems are governance from another view. Al-Ālūsī reports natural powers in nonanimals and choice in animals, but objects that 'creation' already includes powers and this makes 'guided' metaphorical. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī (TABATABAI:6:122-127/r1) distinguishes creational guidance and describes it as directing each kind and individual toward its created perfection, acts, appointed course, and lifespan."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p4", "position": "He grants religious guidance and a path to afterlife blessing.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and al-Jubbāʾī pair worldly gifts with religion and eternal afterlife blessings; al-Nasafī includes happiness in the next life. Ibn Sābiṭ's four animal guidances include knowing God as Lord, mating, livelihood and fearing death. Al-Burūsawī infers all creatures know and glorify God according to their faculties, citing 17:44. Al-Iṣlāḥī adds messengers and books for humanity."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p5", "position": "He fixes destinies and guides creatures through them without departure.", "reasons": "Some exegetes align 20:50 with 87:3 and specify decreed deeds, lifespans and provisions."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p6", "position": "He creates cognitive and motive powers after forming bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares Adam's formed body before the spirit and human developmental stages, citing 15:29 and 23:12–14. Al-Ālūsī objects that creation is broader than bodily assembly and already includes motion and perception."}, {"id": "20:50/q08/p7", "position": "He guides human beings to know His existence and unity.", "reasons": "A view reported by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects dispositionally sought existence with human knowledge of God; he rejects its restriction of the verse without evidence."}]}
{"id": "20:50/q14", "question": "How does this verse connect with other guidance passages and what follows?", "turns_on": "Which other passages illuminate this general proof and its place in the exchange.", "positions": [{"id": "20:50/q14/p1", "position": "It parallels other creation-and-guidance verses and leads from general proof to particular signs.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 87:1–3 and 26:77–78, then says the next verse begins with the earth as a specific proof after the general one. Al-Damghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī connect inspired livelihood and mating to 87:2–3; Asad traces the idea to this early passage. Ibn Kathīr's reported deterministic gloss also cites 87:3. Al-Iṣlāḥī invokes 87:1–3 for Moses' answer. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī (TABATABAI:6:122-127/r1) links God's giving each thing its form and guiding it to 87:2–3."}, {"id": "20:50/q14/p2", "position": "The exchange points to divine signs and the question of God's inaccessible essence.", "reasons": "The Study Quran links Pharaoh's later question to 26:23–24 and cites 3:13,15 for the limits of human description."}]}
{"id": "20:53/q22", "question": "What inward sense is given to the earth, paths, water and plants?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:53/q22/p1", "position": "They signify the bodily faculties, their organs, spiritual perception and their varied states.", "reasons": "Qashani treats earth as bodily realm, paths as eye, ear, nose and other organs, heaven as spirit, rain as perception and aid, and plants as perceptions, actions, properties, states and dispositions."}, {"id": "20:53/q22/p2", "position": "The earth rests bodies; bodies rest worship, hearts rest gnosis, spirits rest love, and inner secrets rest witnessing.", "reasons": "Qushayri presents a sequence of resting places, extending the earth's bodily function through progressively inward spiritual faculties and acts."}]}
{"id": "20:54/q01", "question": "What do the commands to eat and pasture livestock mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the commands describe material use of vegetation, a broader idiom of benefit, or an inward reading.", "positions": [{"id": "20:54/q01/p1", "position": "People may eat the plants and fruits God produced and let their livestock graze on the vegetation.", "reasons": "Yahya, Wahidi, and others connect both uses to the rain-grown plants just described. Kashshaf distinguishes human food from animal fodder; Ibn Ashur says the different plant kinds are distributed between them. Bursawi specifies fruits and grains; Tabari says the plants provide livestock provisions. Ibn Atiyya says the chosen actions are especially desirable and calming. Wahidi cites Ibn Abbas's comparison with 80:27–32. Ibn Jawzi describes turning animals loose in pasture. Qushayri says the provision people can reach gives them strength, while the livestock God provides brings them benefit."}, {"id": "20:54/q01/p2", "position": "Eating extends to every beneficial use of what God produced.", "reasons": "Razi compares Qur'anic idioms of consuming wealth in 2:188 and 4:10."}, {"id": "20:54/q01/p3", "position": "Inwardly, eating means receiving fitting spiritual states and provisions, while grazing livestock concerns the animal faculties and their proper morals and manners.", "reasons": "Qashani lists contentment, patience, knowledge, perceptions, intentions, stations, morals, and gifts among the nourishment."}]}
{"id": "20:54/q05", "question": "What does providing food and pasture show about the care of creatures?", "turns_on": "Whether the provision is described as a practical blessing or as the purpose of the created order.", "positions": [{"id": "20:54/q05/p1", "position": "God provides people with cultivated food and livestock with otherwise unusable plants, allowing people direct and indirect benefit.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the kindness of supplying fodder from surplus people cannot eat. Biqai contrasts cultivated human food with the surplus animals consume. Bursawi notes both direct and indirect livestock benefits; Study Quran points to cattle's benefits in 6:142 and 16:5–7. Alusi and Ibn Ashur distinguish the two uses of vegetation. Qushayri says God prepared livelihoods and provides for both people and the animals they use; people draw strength from accessible provision and benefit from their livestock."}, {"id": "20:54/q05/p2", "position": "All creatures and provisions serve human livelihood and the needs of creatures on their journey to God.", "reasons": "Bursawi reports the Najmiyya claim that sky, water, plants, and livestock were made for human livelihood and would not otherwise have been created. He quotes al-Maghribi's poem that the world exists for its addressee. Biqai says provisions fit every creature across changing conditions until presentation before God."}]}
{"id": "20:69/q06", "question": "What does تَلْقَفْ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:69/q06/p1", "position": "To seize swiftly or swallow, here by mouth.", "reasons": "Hasan specifies its mouth. Jishumi compares laqifa, talaqqafa and iltaqafa; Kisa'i says taking quickly. Qurtubi cites laqif thaqif for a deft person and also wall or basin collapse; Bursevi cites taking by hand or mouth. Razi stresses speed. Tha'labi also glosses it as gulping down and engulfing what the magicians made."}, {"id": "20:69/q06/p2", "position": "The intensive form conveys eager or forceful devouring.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER says Form V makes the staff eagerly snatch by itself; Biqai says omitted tāʾ signals speed; the doubled tāʾ evokes the effort of swallowing."}]}
